known_final_diagnosis: Analysis of pleural fluid showed elevated triglycerides of 319 mg/dL consistent with chylothorax. Flow cytometry of the pleural fluid showed that 3% of total cells were monotypic B cells, expressing CD19, CD20, CD45 and kappa light chain but were negative for CD5 and CD10. The T cells (36% of total cells) showed a CD4:CD8 ratio of 4.8:1, with normal expression of CD5. Cytology of fluid revealed moderately cellular effusion with abundant small lymphocytes mixed with a few reactive mesothelial cells. Findings were consistent with B-cell lymphoma.

report.source_text: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated a right pleural effusion (figure 1). A CT chest was subsequently performed and showed a large right-sided pleural effusion with associated compressive atelectasis and slight mediastinal shift to the left. Additionally, it demonstrated adenopathy in the lower neck and upper thorax, which was increased in size compared with CT scan from 3 years ago. Lymphadenopathy was also noted at the thoracic duct, near the confluence of the left subclavian left internal jugular veins (figure 2).

report.source_text: Following thoracentesis, she had slight improvement in her shortness of breath. She was also started on a fat-free diet. However, she developed re-accumulation of pleural fluid several days later and required second thoracentesis with pigtail catheter placement. Repeat fluid analysis showed decreasing triglycerides to 94 mg/dL and negative cultures. She was discharged in stable condition; pigtail catheter was removed prior to discharge.

clinician.final_diagnosis: Chylothorax caused by Waldenstrom’s macroglobulinaemia with pleural involvement
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 50-year-old woman with known Waldenstrom’s macroglobulinaemia presented with right-sided pleuritic chest pain and progressive dyspnea. Pleural fluid analysis demonstrated elevated triglycerides at 319 mg/dL confirming chylothorax, with flow cytometry revealing monotypic B cells expressing markers consistent with lymphoma, and cytology showing abundant small lymphocytes. Chest imaging identified a large right pleural effusion, compressive atelectasis, mediastinal shift, and thoracic duct lymphadenopathy. Physical exam showed absent breath sounds and palpable cervical and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. After thoracentesis and fat-free diet initiation, the patient had transient symptomatic improvement but required repeat thoracentesis and pigtail catheter placement due to fluid re-accumulation. Follow-up fluid analysis showed decreased triglycerides. She was discharged stable after catheter removal.
